articles.title: These are the 6 worst shoes for walking, according to podiatrists
articles.summary: Whether you're taking a leisurely stroll or commuting to work, doctors say it's important to choose your footwear wisely.
articles.body:
Our experts independently review everything we recommend. If you buy through our links, we may earn commission.

I love the look of a sleek high heel and the effortlessness of a flip-flop as much as the next person, but walking one too many steps in both of these shoes has taught me some painful lessons. That's why I have zero tolerance for uncomfortable, unsupportive footwear these days. I walk a lot — at least four miles every day — and I've learned that choosing the right shoes isn't just about how your feet feel now; the choice can have long-lasting, years-long impacts. Below, podiatrists share the shoes they say aren't ideal for long walks — and what they recommend instead.

New Balance Women's Fresh Foam Arishi V4 Running Shoe

Brooks Women’s Ghost 17 Neutral Running Shoe

Brooks Men’s Ghost 17 Neutral Running Shoe

Altra Men's Escalante 4 Road Running Shoe

Yes, the doctors are coming for your Converse and your Vans . "Completely flat, unsupportive basic canvas shoes don't give your foot anything to work with. No arch support, minimal cushioning and no real structure to keep your foot properly aligned," explains Dr. Mohammad Usman , a board-certified foot and ankle surgeon based in Chicago. The result? Your foot has to work significantly harder with every single step, and that adds up fast. "I see a lot of heel pain, arch pain and tendon issues that trace directly back to this," Usman says.

Dr. David Laurino , a board-certified podiatrist in Arizona, agrees. "Avoid trendy sneakers with flat foot beds that look sporty but don't act the part," he says. "Your feet (and everything above them) soak up the stress, and that's not a good thing."

Sure, you want your toes to breathe, but trekking around in flimsy flip-flops is something every doctor I spoke to warned against . "I don't recommend walking around in flat shoes with flexible soles like flip-flops. If you can fold your shoe in half and have the toe touch the heel, it's probably not supportive enough," says Dr. Katherine Hagmann , an Arizona-based board-certified podiatrist.

Usman also advises steering clear of ultra-thin, flexible styles that offer little support. "People end up gripping with their toes to keep flip-flops on, and over time that can aggravate heel pain, tendon issues, hammertoes and forefoot pain," he says.

Dr. Sari Priesand , a board-certified podiatrist in Michigan, makes the case for saving flip-flops for short boardwalk jaunts even more compelling. "If worn for too long, especially on long walks, flip-flops can lead to blisters or foot irritation. There's also an increased risk of falling or slipping when wearing these types of shoes," she says.

The beauty of a ballet flat lies in its simple, sleek, go-with-anything design, but there's bad news when it comes to these shoes. "Ballet flats typically have zero support and your arches will let you know about it," Laurino warns.

Priesand backs this up, adding that ballet flats have minimal cushioning and shock absorption and prolonged wear can cause blisters. "These types of shoes can worsen things like heel and arch pain, and they can make foot deformities more unstable, which can lead to worsening" of the condition, she says.

You know those popular minimalist sandals that are basically just a flat sole with leather straps? They come back in style year after year, but Usman says they're a bad choice if you'll be on your feet for a while. "Completely flat sandals are usually not great, especially for people with Achilles tendonitis," he says. This type of shoe increases the stretch and load on the tendon, which can lead to pain elsewhere. "The more you strain the Achilles tendon, the more it will directly affect the plantar fascia, the knees, hips, lower back, shoulders and more," Usman says.

On the flip side, shoes with a heel — especially a tall one — won't do if you'll be walking long distances. "High heels can cause increased ankle instability and pain in the balls of the feet. They also tend to run quite narrow and can cause issues like neuroma pain or toe deformities," Priesand warns.

Walking from your car to your office in a pair of pumps may not be an issue, but Usman strongly urges against strutting in heels regularly. "With frequent or prolonged use," he says, comes "calf tightness, achilles irritation, forefoot pain, toe crowding and changes in gait that may affect the ankles, knees, hips or lower back."

Perfectly worn-in jeans and tees ? Good. Worn-down sneakers that are shells of their former selves? Bad, very bad, according to the pros. "If the soles are worn out and the cushioning's dead, you might as well be barefoot on concrete," Laurino says.

Usman also stresses the importance of recognizing when it's time to replace your beloved kicks. "People underestimate this one a lot, so I routinely tell patients to really look at their shoes. The outside may look perfectly fine, but the midsole foam has completely broken down underneath and this is what absorbs impact." His rule of thumb? If you've been wearing the same pair of shoes for over a year and you're on your feet daily, it's probably time to replace them.

So, what shoes are a smarter choice when exploring a new city on foot or trying to hit your step goal for the day? Hagmann says supportive sneakers with firm soles and adequate arch support are your best bet. Laurino adds that walkers should also choose shoes with a wide toe box to accommodate natural foot swelling, as well as thick, solid midsoles to prevent sore feet. And if your dogs tend to sweat a lot, breathable materials are also a must.

articles.title: Notorious Glasgow gangland enforcer Paul Ferris dies aged 62
articles.summary: The criminal-turned-author is believed to have died on Tuesday night after a short illness.
articles.body:
A Glasgow gangland enforcer who wrote books about his underworld experiences has died at the age of 62.

Paul Ferris is believed to have died on Tuesday night at the city's Queen Elizabeth University Hospital after a short illness.

He was cleared of the murder of crime boss Arthur Thompson's son, Arthur Thompson Jnr, in 1992, before being jailed for seven years in 1998 for gun-running.

His first book, The Ferris Conspiracy, was published in 2001.

It was later made into a 2013 film, The Wee Man, featuring Line of Duty star Martin Compston as Ferris.

Photographer Brian Anderson, who first met Ferris for a newspaper assignment in 2002, broke the news of his death on his Naked City Facebook page.

Describing Ferris as a best-selling author and a "former notorious criminal", he wrote: "News of his death will come as a shock to many who knew him throughout the different chapters of his life."

Anderson later told BBC Scotland News: "We got on really well. I found him polite, funny and kind.

"It was a shock to everyone that I remained friends with Paul for 25 years."

Thompson, who had links to the Krays in London, was an old school Glasgow criminal known as The Godfather.

By the early 80s, Ferris had become part of his gang as an enforcer, someone who threatened and, when necessary, meted out violence. He rapidly built a fearsome reputation that extended beyond the city.

The 'scandal' of Scotland's longest gangland trial

But their relationship took a remarkable twist in August 1991 when Arthur "Fat Boy" Thompson Jnr, was shot dead outside the family's Provanmill home.

It was named The Ponderosa after the ranch in the hit US Western television series, Bonanza.

Ferris was arrested as the prime suspect in Thompson Jnr's murder but two others were also incriminated.

His friends Joe "Bananas" Hanlon and Bobby Glover did not live to stand trial.

On the day of Thompson Jnr's funeral both men were found shot dead in a car on the cortege route.

The following year Ferris's trial became, at the time, the longest and most expensive criminal case in Scottish legal history.

More than 300 witnesses gave evidence during the 54-day proceedings, which were estimated to have cost £4m.

The prosecution case relied heavily on the evidence of Dennis Woodman, who claimed Ferris had confessed to the killing while both men were being held in Barlinnie Prison.

Defence lawyers challenged the credibility of the evidence and argued the case against Ferris was deeply flawed.

After more than 24 hours of deliberations, the jury acquitted Ferris of murder and all other charges in 1992.

No-one has ever been convicted of Thompson Jnr's killing.

In 2020 Donald Findlay KC - who defended Ferris in court - told Hey Legal that the case had been the most memorable of his career.

He said: "The trial of Paul Ferris for the murder of Arthur Thompson Jr had virtually all the great characters of Glasgow in that trial one way or another.

"Young Arthur was dead, his father was a witness, Ferris was regarded by the police as the heir apparent to Arthur Thompson Sr.

"We had supergrasses, it just had everything that was going for it.

"I forget how many charges that there were but of course Ferris walked on each and every one of them."

Following his release from prison in 2002 after being jailed on gun-running charges, Ferris turned to writing.

His debut book was made into a movie which starred Martin Compston - who had found fame as a teenager in Ken Loach's Sweet Sixteen - as Ferris.

John Hannah played his arch rival, Tam "The Licensee" McGraw.

The crime boss, who died in 2007 aged 55, had been linked to crimes ranging from drug smuggling to murder for more than three decades.

The movie was shot in London due to problems securing permission from Glasgow City Council and the police to film in Ferris's home city.

Ferris went on to publish two further books, Vendetta and Villains, with crime writer Reg McKay, who died in 2012.

articles.title: Could the Suspected Pneumonic Plague Case in Russia Lead to an Outbreak? Experts Weigh in
articles.summary: The death of a lab technician in Russia from suspected pneumonic plague has sparked global alarm. Could it lead to a bigger outbreak, or a pandemic? Experts explain.
articles.body: News of the mysterious death of a laboratory worker at an anti-plague research facility in Russia has swept the world, sparking concern about the risk of an outbreak, or even a pandemic. The medieval-sounding disease still causes a handful of cases around the world every year — yes, the plague never went away — and it’s fully treatable with antibiotics. However, the lack of information around the scientist’s death and the response from Russian authorities the has some experts on high alert. The 28-year-old woman, who worked as a lab technician at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East, died last week of “pneumonia of undetermined” origin, NBC News reported, citing a Russian official, who did not link her death to her work at the lab. As of Wednesday, Oct. 7, her official cause of death has not been confirmed by Russian authorities. According to the Irkutsk regional governor, Igor Kobsev, no “microorganisms linked to the employee’s professional activities were detected” in her body, NBC News reported. However, a spokesperson for the U.S. State Department State Department said Monday that it was monitoring “reports of a fatal case of suspected pneumonic plague” in Irkutsk. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention have also said they are “closely monitoring reports of a suspected case of pneumonic plague in the Irkutsk region of Russia that resulted in a death.” Pneumonic plague is a severe and often fatal lung infection caused by yersinia pestis, the same bacteria that causes the bubonic plague. It can spread from human to human by inhaling respiratory droplets. The staffer’s death has prompted at least one hospital, where she was treated, to enter quarantine, and nearly 200 people with whom she had contact with are under medical observation, NBC News reported, citing a local official and Russian media. The World Health Organization said on Tuesday that no cases of plague have been reported in the Siberian city of Irkutsk, quoting a response from the Russian government. Russia’s consumer and health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, also said in a statement that “no other infectious disease pathogens were detected among the contacts,” NBC News reported. Testing of the woman’s contacts identified two cases of COVID-19 and two cases of rhinovirus, which causes the common cold, per Rospotrebnadzor. According to Russian authorities, the “sanitary-epidemiological situation” in the Irkutsk region is “stable,” NBC News reported. There are still many questions about the scientist’s death, experts tell TODAY.com. The State Department is encouraging Russian officials to “share accurate information quickly and openly,” a spokesperson said. As the situation unfolds, rumors are circulating rapidly on social media, with many fearing another COVID-level pandemic. Here’s what experts think, and why plague may be not be as concerning. Pneumonic Plague Unlikely to Cause a Pandemic “The plague cannot cause widespread outbreaks the way it once did because we have antibiotics,” Dr. Amesh Adalja, a senior scholar at the Center for Health Security at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, tells TODAY.com. The suspected pneumonic plague case in Russia poses a “very low risk” outside of the country, the WHO said. “At this time, there is no indication of a broader threat to the United States, but CDC and our interagency partners are prepared and will continue to monitor the situation closely,” the CDC said in a statement posted to X on Tuesday. “Yes, the plague killed one-third of Europe’s population during the Middle Ages, but they didn’t even know what caused it,” says Adalja. Bubonic vs. Pneumonic Plague All three types of plague are caused by the same bacteria, yersinia pestis, but affect different parts of the body. Bubonic plague, the most common type, occurs when yersinia pestis infects the lymph nodes, says Adalja. It spreads to people through the bite of a flea carrying the bacteria or contact with infected animals, per the CDC. Septicemic plague is caused by the bacteria entering the bloodstream directly. Pneumonic plague, the rarest type, occurs when yersinia pestis infects the lungs. It’s spread by inhaling respiratory droplets from an infected person, but it can also develop if untreated bubonic or septicemic plague spreads to the lungs, Adalja notes. It’s the most virulent type of plague, per the WHO. “But it’s easily containable,” Adalja says. How Pneumonic Plague Spreads and Treatment Although pneumonic plague can transmit through airborne secretions, it doesn’t spread easily in this way. “It’s not a very efficient mode of transmission. Plague isn’t something that spreads in the manner of a virus. It’s nowhere near as contagious as COVID or influenza,” says Adalja. “It’s difficult to get unless you are in prolonged, direct, close contact with a sufferer,” Dr. Susan Jones, a veterinarian and professor at the University of Minnesota who has investigated plague in Russia, tells TODAY.com. Antibiotics are also highly effective at treating and preventing plague after a person is exposed. “Let’s say it is pneumonic plague. This woman worked at an anti-plague institute. They have post-exposure prophylaxis protocols, antibiotics,” Adalja explains. Ongoing Quarantines in Russia According to Russian media reports, quarantines are in effect at the Siberian hospital where the lab worker died, and 60% of her contacts have been tested so far, NBC News reported. It’s unlikely that potentially exposed contacts would’ve left Irkutsk on flights before being quarantined, Jones adds. Additionally, travel to and from Russia to the U.S. is very limited. Dr. Ashish Jha, the White House’s former COVID response coordinator, told NBC News that if this is an isolated case of pneumonic plague, “it will probably end there.” “Thousands of cases of pneumonic plague occur all over the world every year,” Adalja adds. Rarely do these cause outbreaks. “This is not the Black Death, and this is not COVID,” says Jones. Public Health Experts Are Still Concerned Not all experts are convinced pneumonic plague is to blame for the lab worker’s death. “I don’t even know where ‘plague’ came from, other than that it’s on the door of the building where she worked,” says Adalja. Lisa Morici, Ph.D., an immunologist at the Tulane University School of Medicine, told NBC News that “maybe it’s going to come out that she died from something unrelated and it was just a coincidence” that she was a technician at an anti-plague lab. It’s unclear if the deceased worker handled other pathogens. “It could be something else that’s more scary than plague,” says Adalja. The WHO has requested additional information to clarify the cause of the fatal pneumonia case and “media reports of a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause,” WHO Director-General Dr. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said in a post on X. The Russian government’s response to a potential isolated plague case also raises suspicion among some experts. “When you see contacts being monitored, hospitals being quarantined, the head of their public health agency flying there, that’s not congruent with the response for something as easy to handle as plague,” says Adalja. “What exactly was going on inside that lab that has led to the security services of Russia getting involved?” Jha told NBC News. However, Jones, who has visited anti-plague institutes in Russia, says the aggressive public health response is “normal” and follows protocol that dates back to Soviet times. “There (also) aren’t enough public health personnel to escort 200 people into quarantine, so security services are involved,” Jones explains. Symptoms of Pneumonic Plague After inhaling respiratory droplets from a person infected with pneumonic plague, it can take as little as 24 hours to develop symptoms, according to the CDC. The early signs of pneumonic plague include: FeverChillsWeaknessHeadache These can rapidly develop into pneumonia, leading to: Shortness of breathCoughingChest painBloody mucusRespiratory distress If left untreated, pneumonic plague is usually 100% fatal, per the WHO. The infection can be treated with antibiotics, but these are most effective when given early, within 24 hours of symptom onset, Jones adds. Pneumonic Plague in the US In the U.S., an average of seven cases of plague are reported every year, per the CDC. About 80% of these are bubonic plague. The disease has been in the U.S. since the early 1900s, when infected rats entered the country from ships, says Adalja. The last urban plague epidemic occurred from 1924-1925 in Los Angeles, per the CDC. Since then, the bacteria has spread to wild rodents, and most cases are scattered in rural areas. It’s now endemic to the Western U.S., and most cases are reported in Arizona or New Mexico, says Adalja. In 2025, a man in Arizona died of pneumonic plague after being exposed while working with infected cats, per the CDC. Overall, this type of plague is very rare — and unlike when the novel coronavirus emerged, scientists have the tools to fight it. “People are talking about plague as if it’s the 14th century and not the 21st century,” says Adalja. In the meantime, experts are calling for increased transparency and communication from Russia.

articles.title: Trump claims world’s lowest drug prices. TrumpRx discounts a ‘mixed bag,’ report shows.
articles.summary: Ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, President Donald Trump has increasingly touted his drug pricing deals, claiming the U.S. is now paying the world’s lowest prescription drug prices.
articles.body: Ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, President Donald Trump has increasingly touted his drug pricing deals, claiming the U.S. is now paying the world’s lowest prescription drug prices. “This one thing alone should win us the midterms,” he recently said at the White House. TrumpRx.gov, the public face of his drug pricing discounts, has grown dramatically since its launch in February. What started as a few dozen brand-name drugs now includes a catalog of more than 800 brand-name and generic medications, offering discounts on everything from popular weight loss drugs to treatments for cancer and rheumatoid arthritis. It’s unclear whether the average American has “saved a fortune,” as Trump promised. Prescription drug prices fell by 3.1% over the year ending in July, according to federal inflation data — though experts say it’s too soon to know how much of the drop, if any, can be attributed to Trump’s drug pricing deals. The site has relied on GoodRx’s pricing data and technology to power many of its listings and blends pre-existing discounts from drugmakers with newly negotiated prices. At the Republican midterm convention last month, Trump said, “We went from the highest prescription drug prices, by far, anywhere in the world, to the lowest prescription drug prices anywhere in the world.” A recent analysis from KFF finds that TrumpRx prices are competitive with prices in other countries for a small number of cancer and cholesterol medications. In many cases, Americans aren’t getting the best deals compared with the rest of the world. Take Ozempic. For the average patient in the U.S. paying out of pocket, the blockbuster diabetes drug can cost $349 to more than $1,000 a month. It’s $349 through TrumpRx. Yet in several other wealthy countries, the next-highest price is $190 a month, according to KFF, a nonpartisan research group. Enbrel is an even starker example. A monthly supply of the rheumatoid arthritis drug costs $3,354 through TrumpRx, more than five times the $641 average in the other countries where researchers found prices. Some drugs, however, come out well ahead. Rydapt, a drug used to treat certain blood cancers, costs $2,909 for 56 capsules through TrumpRx — less than half the $5,901 price for the same amount in France, the next-cheapest country. Those disparities run throughout the site, according to the KFF analysis. The report, which didn’t compare TrumpRx savings within the U.S., offers one of the first broad worldwide comparisons of Trump’s drug pricing claims. The analysis looked at 32 brand-name drugs sold through TrumpRx that lacked generic or biosimilar equivalents. Researchers focused on those drugs because patients don’t have the option of switching to cheaper versions, meaning the discounts offered through TrumpRx could have a greater impact on what they pay. The group compared the prices with those in 11 other wealthy countries, including Canada, France, Germany, the Netherlands and the United Kingdom. The prices are current as of Aug. 26. The results were almost evenly split. For 17 of the drugs, the TrumpRx prices were lower than the average prices abroad. For 15, they were higher. But Trump has promised Americans the lowest prices in the world. By that measure, the results were less favorable: Only five were actually the lowest-priced, while 13 were the highest-priced. “It’s kind of a mixed bag,” said Juliette Cubanski, deputy director of the Medicare policy program at KFF, who co-authored the report. “Even with the reductions that may have been agreed to by manufacturers who are listing their drugs on the TrumpRx website, the prices that they’re offering, even at a discount, still continue to be higher than prices in comparable countries.” Drug price discounts vary widely The findings offer an early look at both the promise and the limits of Trump’s approach to lowering drug prices. Americans routinely pay more for prescription drugs than patients in other wealthy countries, even when the medications are made by the same companies. The TrumpRx discounts, the White House says, stem from Trump’s “most favored nation” pricing deals, agreements with drugmakers to charge Americans the lower prices they offer other countries in exchange for tariff relief. But the discounts can vary widely, the analysis found, and they haven’t consistently produced the lowest prices Trump promised. “I’m not surprised by these findings,” said Dr. Benjamin Rome, a primary care physician and health policy researcher at Harvard Medical School. “Any of us who have been following drug prices realized, as soon as TrumpRx was launched, it was a limited number of drugs and it was clear that the prices that were there were not always going to be linked or in any way related to what the prices are in other countries.” It’s a markedly different approach from the one taken by Trump’s predecessor Joe Biden. Rather than use Medicare’s power to negotiate prices for a limited number of costly drugs each year, TrumpRx relies largely on voluntary agreements with individual drugmakers to offer discounted prices directly to consumers. (The exact details of the agreements remain largely confidential, and the White House has declined to disclose them.) TrumpRx doesn’t sell the drugs directly. For many drugs, it sends consumers to manufacturer programs through which they can obtain coupons or discounted cash prices without insurance. That’s not how most people get their prescription drugs. About 9 in 10 Americans have some form of health insurance, meaning many pay for medications through private insurance, Medicare or Medicaid — although discounted cash-pay options have become increasingly popular as insurance has gotten more expensive. The money spent on TrumpRx doesn’t count toward a patient’s copay or deductible. “They’re highly selected products where the manufacturer is willing to offer a discount,” Rome said. “Maybe they’re not the products causing the highest spending in the U.S. in some cases or are products where they were already offering confidential discounts, but now they’re making those discounts more public.” The site now includes several cheaper, generic medications. “But those generics and the low prices for those generics pre-existed the TrumpRx website,” Cubanski said. Direct price comparisons are difficult The KFF analysis doesn’t capture every drug available through TrumpRx, and there are limits to how much can be concluded from it. Antonio Ciaccia, CEO of 46brooklyn Research, a group that tracks drug pricing in the U.S., counts about 80 brand-name drugs currently on TrumpRx, while KFF was able to compare prices for 32. Part of the challenge, Ciaccia said, is that some drugs sold in the U.S. aren’t available in all of the countries KFF examined. That can make direct comparisons difficult. “One of the big differences is the U.S. market does have more products in it than international markets, so that is noteworthy to the extent we have options here in the U.S. rather than a one-size-fits-all treatment approach,” he said. International prices aren’t always perfectly comparable, either, he said. The analysis relied on publicly available prices, which may not include confidential discounts negotiated between foreign governments and drugmakers. Ciaccia also noted that KFF’s 11 comparison countries don’t exactly match the countries used in some of the administration’s international pricing programs. The White House didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. Put the claim to the test Those limitations don’t change the basic comparison at the heart of Trump’s claim: whether the prices offered to Americans match or beat those available abroad. “We wanted to put that claim to the test with this analysis,” Cubanski said. “There is not a clear pattern across the board for higher prices or no consistent pattern across the board for lower prices.” And the administration has increasingly made broader claims that it has accomplished just that. “Over the past year, my administration has reached unprecedented agreements with 26 of the world’s largest pharmaceutical companies, and the rest are all coming in very rapidly, to provide their drugs to Americans at discounts of 60, 70, 80 and even 90% discount,” Trump said last month. Health policy experts hope TrumpRx will ultimately bring U.S. prices down, but they say it’s too soon to know. A concern, however, is that as more drugmakers strike deals, they could also raise prices abroad, narrowing the gap without delivering Americans savings. “It’s not just that the price in the U.S. might come down, but another way of having a lower U.S. price is by having a higher international price, and so it could be the case that if we do this comparison again in a year, we might find that TrumpRx are lower than international prices,” Cubanski said.

articles.title: Hoda Kotb Says She’s Always ‘Rushing.’ Jonathan Haidt Says to Change 2 Things on Her Phone
articles.summary: On the Making Space podcast, psychologist and bestselling author Jonathan Haidt gives Hoda Kotb advice for reducing distractions and stress and reclaiming attention.
articles.body: In a world where the news is 24/7 and we’re constantly connected, it can feel like we’re being pulled in all directions, all the time. Hoda Kotb says this constant pull on our attention is why she created her podcast. On the October 6 episode of the Making Space podcast, social psychologist and bestselling author Jonathan Haidt asked Hoda what she hopes people get from listening. “I feel like people need to make space in their life and slow down,” she replied. “I feel like I was on a dead sprint.” Her answer prompts Haidt to read her a quote from Marcus Aurelius about distraction: “Do external things distract you? Then make time for yourself to learn something worthwhile. Stop letting yourself be pulled in all directions.” It resonated with Hoda, who has been vocal about her personal struggle to be present and not feel like she is constantly rushing. “I’ve been saying this to myself, even on small things, like when I’m eating and I’m standing up and I’m wolfing it down…slow,” she said. “I’m calmer, and I feel like with everything, it’s a tap the brakes and slow down, and everything’s coming at us this way.” Haidt recognizes the role technology has played in putting “time pressure on every moment” “If I had to pick the one thing that has changed since 2006 … one of the most universal — we’re all facing it — is just if you ramp up the time pressure on every moment of everyone’s day, life changes for the worse,” he said. He used young people as the most extreme example, saying social media consumes hours of their day, forcing everything else to get squeezed into the remaining time. But it’s a problem that spans generations. “It’s not just the social media. We’re being texted. People get Slack. It’s LinkedIn. It’s everything,” he said. “If we all have hundreds of things coming in every day, that means we are always way behind. We never have three hours to just think or be or experience.” Hoda says this is the reason for her 4:30 am wakeup call. “If I don’t get up at 4:30 to take an hour, I don’t have that hour,” she said. Haidt’s response is simple: “That’s right. The world will take it from you. Your attention is the most precious thing you have.” “There is no limit to the amount of money that you can make in the course of your life,” he continued, “but you will never be able to get more attention than what you can have in the course of a day.” So, what can we actually do about it? “Don’t give it away for free,” he said. He explained that many people check notifications immediately after waking and again before bed because they don’t want to miss anything. “If you commit yourself to not missing anything, then you’re committing yourself to always being interrupted and to never being present and to missing everything in life.” He says cutting back on this distraction starts with making some simple changes on your phone. “These two are incredibly powerful in giving you a lot more attention,” he said. Tip #1: Turn off notifications Haidt’s first piece of advice is to turn off certain notifications. He conducts this experiment with all of his MBA students at NYU Stern School of Business: Find your most distracting apps. Open “screen time” and look at the five apps sending you the most notifications.Pick one or two to turn off. He specifically recommends doing this for email, social media or any news site. “You should consume the news once or twice a day, not 30 times a day,” he said.Conduct a 1-week check in: See how you feel after one week. At the one-week check in with his students, “nothing bad happened to anyone. They didn’t actually miss anything,” he said. “A lot of them said, ‘I felt lighter. I felt more present, like I could be in conversations more.’” This experiment has “the weight taken off of their attention,” he said. “They’re guarding their attention.” Tip #2: Identify your “slot machine apps” Haidt shared another practical rule: Remove addictive apps from your phone. “Do not have slot machine apps on your phone,” he said. “Just delete it from your phone.” Slot machine apps are “anything that rewards you on a variable ratio schedule. So, that’s especially all the social media sites, video games...” he explained. “For a while, I had crypto. I would check [constantly]. It was insane and I was addicted. So that’s a slot machine app.” He’s not saying that people need to quit these apps entirely, but he does say they should not be at your fingertips all day long. Instead, he recommends accessing them from a laptop. Removing them from your phone is “incredibly powerful in giving you a lot more attention,” he said.

articles.title: People on weight-loss drugs report fingernails falling off as researchers uncover surprising link
articles.summary: Nail discoloration was reported by 46% of GLP-1 users versus 17% of non-users, while scalp inflammation accompanied hair loss in most medication users studied.
articles.body: People taking GLP-1 medications for obesity or diabetes experience nail detachment and hair loss at significantly higher rates than people with similar overall health who do not take GLP-1s. That's according to research presented Oct. 1 at the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology (EADV) Congress 2026 in Vienna, Austria. Two studies evaluated 575 users of GLP-1 (glucagon-like peptide-1) drugs and a control group of 1,329 non-users, all of whom had type 2 diabetes, obesity or both. Participants were recruited across France, the U.S, Brazil and Mexico. POPULAR WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS FACE NUMEROUS LAWSUITS OVER RARE ‘EYE STROKE’ LINKED TO VISION LOSS In the primary study examining nail health, 39% of GLP-1 users reported nail detachment compared with 9% of non-users. Discoloration of the nails affected 46% of GLP-1 users versus 17% in the control group. Overall, two-thirds of GLP-1 users (66%) reported experiencing at least one nail disorder, compared with 53% of the control group. Researchers found that weight loss alone did not explain the difference. Even when researchers looked only at people who lost weight, those taking GLP-1s were still more likely to have these problems. After adjusting for existing dermatological conditions and nutritional deficiencies, nail detachment and discoloration remained two to three times more frequent among the medication group. "Until now, nail changes associated with GLP-1 therapies had essentially been anecdotal," study author Dr. Charles Taïeb, a clinical dermatologist at Necker University Hospital in Paris, said in a press release. "Our findings show a clear association, but they also underline an important point: Not everything that happens during GLP-1 treatment is necessarily caused by the treatment itself." POPULAR GLP-1 WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS LINKED TO POTENTIALLY DEADLY BRAIN DISORDER In another study evaluating hair and scalp conditions among the same group of participants, 50% of GLP-1 users reported unusual hair loss compared with 34% of the control group. After starting treatment, 26% of GLP-1 users reported hair loss or thinning, compared with 12% of those not taking the drugs. Loss of hair volume was also more common, affecting 42% of GLP-1 users compared with 19% of those not taking them, the study found. Scalp redness was reported around three times as frequently in GLP-1 users, and hair loss among users was typically accompanied by inflammatory scalp symptoms such as itching, scaling or redness, the researchers noted. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES "This suggests that what is happening on the scalp may go beyond the classical shedding seen after rapid weight loss and involve an inflammatory component," said study author Dr. Bruno Halioua, a Paris dermatologist, in the release. "Scalp inflammation was the rule rather than the exception, which clinicians do not currently look for and which may be treatable." CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER Halioua stated that patients experiencing these symptoms should consult a physician rather than stopping their medication, noting that the changes are typically not serious enough to warrant discontinuing treatment. The authors emphasized that because both studies relied on patient-reported data and looked at them at a single point in time, the findings only show associations and cannot prove that the medications caused these effects. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Roughly half of the GLP-1 users surveyed reported having nail issues prior to starting treatment. The research team is planning further studies to determine when these changes occur, what may be causing them and whether they go away over time. Fox News Digital reached out to GLP-1 manufacturers requesting comment.

articles.title: Rhondda father 'crumbled' when daughter died after fall at school
articles.summary: Olivia-Grace's father says his world crumbled when his daughter died after falling in school.
articles.body:
"I know I'm biased because she was mine, but she was the best human I've ever met," says Aaron John Huxter of his daughter Olivia-Grace.

The 33-year-old says his "entire world crumbled from a phone call" when he was told his eight-year-old daughter had fallen at her school in Rhondda Cynon Taf.

He was more than an hour's drive away, and when he was just around the corner, he was told they had restarted her heart.

Aaron says he got out of his van and collapsed in shock, before being taken to the ambulance where a paramedic told him: "We've stabilised her but you have a very, very sick little girl."

Not long after, they were told Olivia-Grace's brain could not recover. Aaron and Olivia-Grace's mum, Melanie, stayed with her at Cardiff's University Hospital of Wales until she died on 8 October 2025 .

"It kills me that the worst day of my life was just a normal Wednesday for everyone else," he says.

"She went off to school, just as she did every day, and then never came home."

The coroner's report is still outstanding, and they are not sure they will find out the exact cause of Olivia-Grace's death, but Aaron says he does not blame anyone.

He described his daughter as a miracle who "defied the odds" as she had Atrioventricular septal defect (AVSD), underwent heart repair at six months old and overcame pneumonia at five.

"I'm sorry you never got to meet her," Aaron says, "that's how I feel when I tell everyone about her.

"Nothing can ever prepare you to lose your child. Not just to lose your daughter, but to lose your entire reason. Trying to move forward from losing a child, it's the most difficult thing in the world.

"The pain I feel now, I know I will always feel, but I know it's completely necessary. I wouldn't want anything that would stop me from missing her, she was so incredible she deserves to be missed every day.

"I'm just grateful it was me, I'm the one she chose."

Aaron is part of a men's bereavement campaign run by the charity 2wish , which supports those affected by sudden death in young people.

It aims to encourage more open conversations about grief.

"The general standard is that the mum would be the one really struggling, and the dad is there as the strong one," he says.

"I wish I could say that's how it happened but we just went around it in a completely different way, we leant on each other when we both needed it."

Aaron says men could find it difficult to express their feelings "as it's bred in us that it exposes weakness or vulnerability".

"As a man you could just bottle it up... it will fester and grow and it can very quickly turn very, very dark," he says.

"I won't sit here and lie and say I haven't had those thoughts, because I have. The day we lost Olivia was the darkest day of my life.

"You feel like your main job in life is to protect your child and keep your child safe, and I wasn't able to do that.

"As a dad you can feel like you failed, even though it's completely out of your hands, you have still had to bury your child."

Aaron says he tries to embrace the darker times that come with his grief.

"Whether you're wailing or it's a little cry on the way home. I feel it necessary, it's Olivia-Grace coming through."

He recalls receiving a 2wish memory box the day after Olivia died, which gave them a "tiny light in a dark time" and included thumbprints and elephant cuddly toys.

One elephant was left with Olivia-Grace, and the family kept the other elephant, because "elephants never forget".

The family was also assigned 2wish caseworker Jo who helped them with arranging Olivia-Grace's funeral, and continues to provide support through monthly coffee mornings and regular check-ins.

Aaron says the coffee mornings were a time when he could be vulnerable.

"I put on a face of Aaron the funny one, who makes everyone laugh. In that room I don't need to put on a front, they know the pain I'm feeling.

"Everyone's process with grief is completely different, but with how easy we find it to speak about our grief and Olivia-Grace, we find that it helps others to speak.

"I always make sure to see a picture of their child, to ask about their child," he added.

"I know there are families out there that feel [grief] needs to be something very personal and very private, but it really doesn't."

Describing what Olivia-Grace was like, Aaron says she had a "sixth sense" for people having a bad day and was a natural at lifting people up, greeting strangers with a smile and hug when they needed it.

"She would make the angriest bloke smile, and the saddest lady laugh, that's just who she was... she was who everyone went to when they needed to be fixed."

He says she was a huge part of her school, who are marking her death with an "Olivia-Grace day" celebration, which Aaron and Melinda will be attending.

But passing one year since her death brings painful emotions.

"Because it's the first, we just don't know what to expect or how to react," he says.

"Once that day passes, I can no longer say I lost my daughter in October. I will have to say October 2025.

"For me, every day that goes by, it's not just another day where I haven't had her... it's an extra day I haven't seen her."

He says: "She wasn't just my responsibility, she was the reason I hit any goals, she was the reason I looked forward to finishing work, she was at the forefront of everything I did.

"That wasn't just me, that was her brothers, her sisters, her mum. She was just the centre.

"She changed me for the better, she made me a lot softer. She made me vulnerable, I never knew I could be this vulnerable.

"If she can't do it, I want as many people to know about Olivia-Grace."

articles.title: Watchdog and critics raise concerns over reliability of NHS medical records
articles.summary: Victims of disgraced brain surgeon Sam Eljamel have complained of "significant gaps" in their records and said they often do not reflect the reality of their care.
articles.body:
Concerns have been raised about the reliability of the NHS medical records systems used in Scotland.

Their accuracy has been questioned by the public services watchdog and critics warned there were doubts about their reliability in safety investigations and court cases.

Victims of disgraced brain surgeon Sam Eljamel have complained of "significant gaps" in their records and said they often do not reflect the reality of their care.

The Scottish government said it took the concerns raised seriously and was engaging with health boards over ways to improve the reliability of patient records.

There are millions of patient records in Scotland, which contain information about your health, care and treatment.

When things go wrong they are relied upon for investigations and legal challenges.

However, there is no central NHS system where these records are kept and a number of concerns about their accuracy have been raised in recent years.

The long-running Scottish Hospitals Inquiry's probe into patient safety issues at Glasgow's Queen Elizabeth University Hospital campus has heard concerns about missing medical records and about how information was recorded.

The issue of accurate medical records will also feature heavily in the recently started public inquiry into the actions of Eljamel at Dundee's Ninewells Hospital.

Alan Ogilvie, who was operated on by Eljamel in 1995, is spokesman for the Patients Action Group which campaigned for the inquiry.

Ogilvie said many of those affected had found their official medical records "often don't match their lived reality".

He added: "We see significant gaps where complications occurred, and narratives that seem massaged to suit the clinician's reputation rather than the patient's history.

"When the 'official' computer record says one thing, but our own letters and memories prove another, you have to ask: Is the system there to record the truth, or to protect the institution?

"If we cannot trust the records from the past, how can we trust the lessons they claim to be learning for the future?"

The Scottish Public Services Ombudsman (SPSO) has often raised the issue of accurate medical records.

Last month, NHS Lothian was criticised by the watchdog for not carrying out a Significant Adverse Event Review into the death of a patient from a blood infection at the Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh.

These included four occasions where it said in the clinical notes that the doctor in charge had asked for a microbiology report - but there was no evidence of such a report in the patient's clinical records.

'Sys­tems don't seem to talk to each other'

The sharing of information from patient records between NHS boards is the focus of an ongoing fatal accident inquiry (FAI) into the death of two-month-old Michael Wilson at the Royal Aberdeen Children's Hospital.

The inquiry has heard from a doctor who said he would have advised against operating on Michael if he had known, from the child's medical records, about an inherited heart condition.

It had been the suspected cause of death of Michael's older brother in Glasgow two years previously.

At an earlier hearing the Press and Journal reported that Sheriff Christine McCrossan said: "It's almost verging into a public inquiry situation - something as fundamental as the medical records situation in the country.

"These boards are inde­pend­ent and they set up com­puter sys­tems that don't seem to talk to each other."

Labour MSP Daniel Johnson said medical records were an invaluable resource for medics.

"But at the point they are being relied upon by other public agencies, including the Crown Office, we need absolute clarity about their reliability," he added.

"Important questions need to be answered about how the Crown Office, the Central Legal Office and other publicly funded bodies assess the reliability of patient medical records and the user protocols which support their use."

A Scottish government spokesperson said: "We recognise that accurate, complete and accessible patient records are essential to safe care, continuity of treatment and effective investigation of adverse events.

"NHS boards are responsible for the electronic patient record systems they operate and for ensuring that clinical information is accurate, secure, accessible and appropriately governed."

The added a range of assurance mechanisms to support the reliability of patient record systems were used including national standards and data quality controls.

The spokesperson said: "We take the concerns raised from recent inquiries seriously and continue to engage with boards to consider findings and any recommendations for improving the reliability of patient records to support safe and effective care."

articles.title: The secret to a good night’s rest? Let sleeping dogs lie ... next to you
articles.summary: A surprising new study found that people who sleep near their dogs don’t experience disrupted sleep. If anything we humans are the ones disturbing our dogs’ sleep.
articles.body: There’s no feeling in the world like cuddling up at night with your pooch, even when we think they’re messing up our sleep by hogging space, stealing covers and yapping at random sounds. A surprising new study found that people who sleep near their dogs don’t experience disrupted sleep. If anything, the University of Toronto researchers discovered, we humans are the ones disturbing our dogs’ sleep. And we feel safer sleeping with our dogs, hinting at “a deeper evolutionary history” between humans and dogs, said study co-author Ming Fei Li, who was a graduate student of evolutionary anthropology during the research. Activity trackers similar to Fitbits monitored the nighttime activity of 25 human volunteers and their 38 dogs in southern Ontario to monitor how each affected the other’s sleep. The study, which was published Wednesday in PLOS One, was conducted during the Covid pandemic as part of a larger project comparing the activity patterns of socialized wolves and domestic dogs. For four weeks, the humans wore the devices on their wrists while the dogs, all huskies and malamutes with no health problems, wore them on their collars. Most dogs slept on the bed or in the same room as their humans. A few dogs slept in different rooms, said anthropology researcher Lavania Nagendran, who was also a study author. Using the activity trackers, they analyzed “objective sleep measures” of the people and their dogs, including sleep duration and sleep quality, Nagendran said. The human volunteers also self-reported their sleep quality in an accompanying survey. Though half of the people, particularly those who slept with more than one dog at a time, reported interrupted sleep, the activity tracker data found that sharing a bed with their dogs didn’t affect how well or how long the pups or their humans slept. “When we looked at the subjective, or people’s perceived, sleep, we saw that there were people who reported poor sleep if they had multiple dogs,” Nagendran said. “But, again, that wasn’t seen in the devices.” When they observed “synchronized activity states” with the devices, they found that humans and dogs became active around the same time while they were sleeping but that it was the humans who moved first and disturbed their dogs, not the other way around, Li said. That contradicts a 2020 study that found dogs influenced human movement more than humans influenced dog movement during the night. The researchers also found it made no difference whether people’s dogs slept directly in the bed with them or in a nearby area. There were limitations to the study, including the small group of volunteers, which consisted of more women than men, and a lack of variation in dog breeds, Li said. Previous research on co-sleeping with a dog has shown a link between poorer sleep and owning a pet and found that people sleep well with a dog nearby, but not in the bed. A 2023 study published in the journal Human-Animal Interactions found a link between pet ownership and poorer sleep, while a 2017 Mayo Clinic study found people slept better with a dog nearby except when the dog slept on the bed with them. Dogs may actually improve our sleep habits by forcing us to adjust to consistent bedtime schedules — as anyone with a sleepy, whining dog can confirm. Dogs are “zeitgebers”; that is, they provide cues about when it’s time to eat, take a walk or go to sleep, said W. Christopher Winter, a sleep medicine expert at Charlottesville Neurology & Sleep Medicine in Virginia. “Dogs want things done on a certain rhythm, and that can be really positive for people who struggle with that,” Winter said. Most sleep research shows that “creating internal consistency” around sleep habits may matter more than the amount of sleep a person gets, he said. “It’s the consistent nature of sleep that is really important, and I think dogs do a wonderful job of creating that,” he said. Not all dogs are good sleepmates, though. A large dog, for example, may take up a lot of bed space and “hog the sheets,” while dogs of any size can wake during the night when they hear random sounds or see flashes of light, said Winter, who wasn’t involved in the study. Some dogs, particularly dogs with upper airway abnormalities like pugs, Boston terriers and French bulldogs, may snore loudly, which could disturb their human companions, he said. “Some of the worst snoring and sleep apnea I’ve ever heard has been a dog at 4 o’clock in the afternoon sleeping when you’re watching a football game,” Winter joked.

articles.title: The new 'mommy's little helper' is a $175-a-month injectable to fight exhaustion
articles.summary: Exhausted moms are taking NAD+ for more energy and less brain fog. But has the science caught up with the hype?
articles.body:
As a working 30-something raising two young kids, I'm perpetually tired, and it shows. My eyes tend to look sunken, my skin wouldn't exactly be described as "glowy," and I rarely have energy to do my hair. But on social media, my fellow moms are suddenly looking perky.

In TikTok videos and Instagram carousels, these women show before-and-after photos in which they go from ragged to refreshed, seemingly overnight. Their secret? NAD+ supplements and injections — the new "mommy's little helper" when it comes to battling the all-encompassing fatigue of motherhood.

"I feel better than I have in 10 years," says Tia Collis, a 43-year-old mother of two from Florida, who injects herself with the anti-aging treatment.

Claims like these are why taking NAD+ (nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide) and its precursors NMN (nicotinamide mononucleotide) and NR (nicotinamide riboside) is catching on beyond longevity bros and biohackers, trickling down to tired moms in their 30s and 40s.

As Dr. Mindy Goldman , the chief clinical officer of Midi Health, tells me, NAD+ is a coenzyme found naturally in nearly every cell in our body, helping maintain their function and convert food into energy. As we age, our NAD+ levels decrease, which may make it harder for cells to produce energy and repair damage. Women like Collis inject themselves with NAD+, hoping to bring back the youthful energy they need in the trenches of motherhood, along with sharper focus and less brain fog.

"There's growing interest in whether supporting NAD+ levels may help with things women care about, like energy, metabolism and brain health," Goldman says.

That possibility is what initially drew Collis to try injectable NAD+ for herself. Like me, Collis' life is a constant game of balance. She's not only raising her two kids, who are 11 and 3, but also working full-time as a realtor, entrepreneur and content creator. All this juggling is made more challenging by the fact that she has Hashimoto's disease, an autoimmune disorder that impacts the thyroid and can cause fatigue and sluggishness.

"I was having to take a nap every day," she recalls.

Not anymore. On Instagram , Collis posted videos of herself sticking a needle full of injectable NAD+ into her leg , showing her glowing results and saying she feels like she's "25 again." Her fatigue and brain fog have cleared, she tells me. She was a big enough fan that she eventually became an affiliate of the company she buys from to spread the word.

"It [makes] me feel more human and less like a 42-year-old midlife zombie," she tells her audience in one video.

Videos like Collis's are frequent discussion topics in mom circles, like my group chats with my friends with young kids, where we constantly trade ideas to make it through our hectic days. When one of my friends began taking NAD+ pills, we all eagerly awaited her results like she was our personal guinea pig.

But the promise of a shot, powder or pill turning me into a supermom comes with a price tag: Injectables can run $175 for a month's supply , powder supplements, which typically contain NAD+ precursors like NMN, can cost about $120 and even the pills are around $69 , raising the question of whether the results are really worth the cost.

Well, maybe, says Goldman. She cautions that supplemental NAD+ is still being studied. So while we understand a lot about what it naturally does in our cells, we don't have robust human research on the benefits of boosting the co-enzyme's levels.

"Social media has helped generate a lot of excitement around NAD+, but the claims can sometimes get ahead of the science," says Goldman.

Naturopathic medicine specialist Jacob Hill tells the Cleveland Clinic that a lot of interest in these supplements comes from "the potential anti-aging and longevity benefit." But, he adds, "research in this area is still developing. The long-term benefits and risks are unclear until more research is available."

From what Goldman has seen, there does seem to be a fair number of women who report feeling more energetic and mentally sharp, and she understands why these benefits would be appealing to mothers of young kids — and perimenopausal women — specifically. However, she cautions against believing some of the more over-the-top claims.

"Be cautious of promises around reversing aging, dramatic weight loss or eliminating fatigue, and look for information that reflects both what we know and what we're still learning," she says.

Goldman is supportive if people want to give the supplement a try. But she also wants moms to engage in other ways to beat burnout, like getting regular exercise, prioritizing sleep and eating nutritious food.

"It may be one tool women are interested in exploring, but it shouldn't replace addressing the underlying reasons they may be feeling that way," she says.

Ultimately, while NAD+ may not be a silver bullet that will change my entire life, it can be one piece of a broader plan for balance and self-care. After trying the pills, my friend told us she decided not to continue because the small energy boost she felt wasn't worth the high cost. But those who do notice a big difference may encourage others to give it a shot.

Collis tells me that while she always advises her followers to consult their doctors before starting any vitamins or supplements, she also wants women like her to know there are ways to feel better.

"There are tools to help the fatigue and brain fog," she says. "You don't have to suffer like that."

articles.title: India's diabetes burden is creating another problem: The growing threat to eyesight
articles.summary: A person can be reading this story clearly, driving to work, watching television and using a phone normally, while diabetes may already be damaging the
articles.body: A person can be reading this story clearly, driving to work, watching television and using a phone normally, while diabetes may already be damaging the blood vessels at the back of the eye.That is what makes diabetic eye disease particularly difficult to spot. Diabetic retinopathy can develop without pain or obvious changes in vision in its early stages. By the time blurred vision, dark spots or floaters appear, damage to the retina may already be significant.And with diabetes becoming increasingly common in India, the concern is no longer limited to blood sugar, heart health or kidney disease. The eyes are another part of the body that can pay the price of prolonged uncontrolled blood glucose.The ICMR-INDIAB national study, published in The Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology, estimated that 11.4% of Indian adults had diabetes and another 15.3% had prediabetes. The study analysed data from more than 113,000 people across India. Researchers also found that diabetes was more common in urban areas than rural areas.For the eyes, one of the biggest concerns is diabetic retinopathy.What happens inside the eye?The retina is the light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye. It needs a steady blood supply, which comes through a dense network of tiny blood vessels.Persistently high blood sugar can damage these vessels. They may swell, leak fluid or blood, and in more advanced disease, abnormal blood vessels can develop. This can affect the retina and eventually threaten vision.“Chronic uncontrolled blood sugar can damage the minute blood vessels providing blood supply to the retina, which is responsible for vision in the eye,” said Dr Mahipal Singh Sachdev, Chairman and Managing Director, Centre for Sight Group of Hospitals.The problem is that the damage does not necessarily announce itself immediately.A national survey conducted across 21 districts in India found diabetes in 11.8% of people aged 50 years and above in the surveyed population. The study also assessed diabetic retinopathy and sight-threatening diabetic retinopathy, highlighting the scale of the eye-care burden among people living with diabetes.The eye may not hurt when damage beginsThis is one of the most easily missed parts of diabetic eye disease.“By the time a patient notices blurred vision, dark spots and floaters in their eyes, significant damage could have already been done to the retina,” said Dr Abhishek Dave, Principal Consultant – Ophthalmology, Max Super Specialty Hospital, Noida.Early diabetic retinopathy may cause no noticeable symptoms. That means waiting for vision to become blurry is not a reliable way to know whether the retina is healthy.As the condition progresses, people may experience blurred or distorted vision, dark spots or floaters, difficulty seeing at night and, in severe cases, sudden vision loss.Diabetes can also increase the risk of other eye problems, including cataract and glaucoma, adding to the potential impact on vision.The longer diabetes stays uncontrolled, the greater the concernThe risk is not simply about having diabetes for a short period. Duration of the disease and the degree of blood-sugar control matter.Research from the Chennai Urban Rural Epidemiology Study found that for every five-year increase in diabetes duration, the risk of diabetic retinopathy increased about 1.89 times. The same study found that for every 2% increase in HbA1c, the risk increased by a factor of about 1.7.This is why blood sugar is not the only number people with diabetes need to keep track of. Blood pressure and cholesterol also matter.“Those who have diabetes should control their blood sugar and blood pressure by means of necessary medication, a healthy diet, and physical activity,” Dr Dave said.Why an eye test matters even when vision seems fineA routine eye examination can detect changes that a person cannot see or feel themselves.Dr Sachdev recommends that people with diabetes keep track of blood sugar, blood pressure and cholesterol, while getting their eyes examined as frequently as advised by their doctor.“The most important thing though is that people with diabetes should not postpone visiting the doctor until they have eye problems,” Dr Dave said. “A regular eye doctor visit at least once a year can reveal any changes in the patient's health and prevent vision loss.”The exact frequency of screening can vary depending on the type of diabetes, duration of disease, existing retinal changes and other health factors. People who have already been diagnosed with diabetic retinopathy may need more frequent monitoring.Much of the serious vision loss can be preventedThe frightening part of diabetic retinopathy is its ability to remain hidden. But that also points to one of the biggest opportunities: early detection.Diabetic retinopathy does not automatically mean that a person will lose their sight. Blood-sugar and blood-pressure control, regular medical care and timely retinal screening can help reduce the risk of severe vision loss. Treatment options are also available when retinal disease is detected.For India, the challenge is particularly large because diabetes itself affects millions of adults and is continuing to expand across different parts of the country. The ICMR-INDIAB study found that diabetes prevalence varied substantially between states and warned that the epidemic was still increasing in many parts of the country.So the next time someone with diabetes says, “My eyesight is perfectly fine, so I don't need an eye check-up,” that may be exactly when the check-up matters most.The retina does not always send an early warning.And sometimes, the first sign that something is wrong is not what a person sees, but what an eye examination finds before they notice anything at all.

articles.title: Diet soda vs water: Study reveals which beverage is better for weight loss
articles.summary: A two-year randomized trial found that diet drinks with aspartame, sucralose and acesulfame potassium matched water for weight loss outcomes.
articles.body: Diet drinks containing sugar substitutes were found to be as effective as water for supporting weight loss in overweight or obese adults, according to a two-year randomized trial. The study, led by the University of Liverpool, England, included 493 participants ranging from 18 to 65 years old, all of whom had a body mass index (BMI) between 27 and 35 (overweight or obese). Half of them received 22.3 ounces of water each day, and the other half received the same amount of soda with non-nutritive sweeteners (about two cans) for a 104-week period. YOUR BRAIN MAY BE TRICKING YOU INTO LIKING ARTIFICIAL SWEETENERS, STUDY FINDS The group assigned to NNS drinks could choose from a variety of diet sodas, low-calorie fruit drinks and flavored waters. The primary sweeteners used were aspartame, acesulfame potassium and sucralose. After two years, people drinking diet beverages had lost about 10.6 pounds, while those drinking water lost about 8.2 pounds. People in both groups kept off a meaningful amount of weight for two years, even during the last year when they no longer had regular weight-management support, the researchers stated. Both groups lost inches around their waists and hips and reduced body fat, but there was no meaningful difference between people drinking diet beverages and those drinking water. POPULAR ARTIFICIAL SWEETENER LINKED TO POTENTIALLY DANGEROUS HEART RISK Additionally, total cholesterol remained within the healthy range in both groups. The findings were published in the British Journal of Nutrition. "The study does not show that diet beverages themselves caused the weight loss," Alix Turoff, a registered dietitian in New York City, told Fox News Digital. "Everyone in the study was participating in a structured weight-management program that included nutrition counseling, behavioral support and physical activity recommendations." CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES Turoff, who was not involved in the study, noted that the main value of including diet beverages comes down to substitution, "not that these beverages have a magical metabolic effect." Notably, the study compared diet beverages with water — rather than with sugar-sweetened drinks — making it a test of whether the sugar substitutes themselves appeared to hinder weight loss efforts. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "If someone normally drinks 250 calories of regular soda and switches to zero-calorie soda, then they’re saving calories," she added. The dietitian emphasized that these findings don’t mean water and diet soda are nutritionally identical. "The study did not find significant between-group differences in hunger or sugar intake at the end of the trial, which is relevant because one common concern is that artificial sweeteners may increase appetite or lead to compensatory eating," Turoff said. "I would still recommend water as the primary hydration choice, but I don’t think people need to be afraid of diet drinks because they think they will automatically prevent fat loss or cause weight gain." CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER There were some limitations with the research, including that it was conducted at one location in England. Race and ethnicity data were not collected, which limits the generalizability of the findings. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Only 220 of the 493 participants who started treatment completed the 104-week assessment. The second-year extension was also voluntary, meaning those who continued may have been more motivated or more likely to stick with the program, Turoff noted. While the trial was funded by the American Beverage Association, the study authors stated that the association did not participate in the study design, data analysis or interpretation of the results.

articles.title: Médica é investigada por sugerir retenção de petistas em eleição | G1
articles.standfirst: Órgão informou que adotou medidas preventivas para garantir o livre exercício do voto no segundo turno. Médica foi afastada das funções enquanto o caso é apurado.
articles.summary: A Procuradoria Regional Eleitoral de Goiás investiga a conduta da médica Marcella Segato, afastada após sugerir a retenção de pacientes petistas para impedir o voto nas eleições.
articles.body:
A Procuradoria Regional Eleitoral em Goiás (PRE-GO) pediu a investigação do caso da médica Marcella Segato de Sousa Melo, suspeita de orientar outros profissionais de saúde a não dar alta a pacientes durante o primeiro turno das eleições porque, segundo ela, “a maioria é petista”. A ginecologista e obstetra foi afastada das funções no Hospital Municipal da Mulher e Maternidade Célia Câmara (HMMCC), em Goiânia , enquanto o caso é apurado.

Segundo a PRE-GO, o caso foi encaminhado ao órgão do Ministério Público Eleitoral responsável pela apuração. A Procuradoria informou ainda que foram adotadas medidas preventivas para garantir o livre exercício do voto no segundo turno das eleições.

O procedimento tem acesso restrito e, por isso, a PRE-GO não informou quais medidas preventivas foram adotadas nem deu detalhes sobre a apuração. O órgão afirmou que não antecipa qualquer avaliação sobre os fatos investigados.

Em nota enviada ao g1 , Marcella pediu desculpas pelas mensagens, mas afirmou que a orientação não resultou em conduta inadequada e que nenhuma paciente teve a alta atrasada ou negada.

“Da mesma forma, nenhuma avaliação levou em conta preferência política. O voto é secreto e deve ser respeitado, sem qualquer tipo de retaliação”, afirmou.

Médica é suspeita de orientar funcionários a ‘não dar alta para petistas’ em dia de eleição — Foto: Reprodução/TV Anhaguera

Hospital Municipal da Mulher e Maternidade Célia Câmara, em Goiânia, está com inscrições abertas para vagas de contratação imediata e cadastro de reserva — Foto: Divulgação/Maternidade Célia Câmara

A mensagem foi enviada no dia 2 de outubro, dois dias antes do primeiro turno, em um grupo privado que reúne profissionais médicos da maternidade.

“Quem estiver na enfermaria sábado e domingo, não dar alta para ninguém, a maioria é petista”, escreveu Marcella.

Prints da conversa mostram que 12 participantes reagiram à mensagem com emojis de risada, sinal de positivo e bandeira do Brasil. Um dos participantes respondeu “combinado”.

Até o momento, não há confirmação de que alguma paciente tenha tido a alta atrasada ou negada em razão de preferência política. Marcella afirmou que todas as pacientes foram avaliadas e liberadas exclusivamente com base em critérios clínicos.

“Essas mensagens, porém, não se transformaram em conduta nem resultaram em procedimentos inadequados. Nenhuma paciente teve a alta atrasada ou negada”, afirmou a médica.

Marcella é chefe da ginecologia e obstetrícia do HMMCC e foi afastada das funções enquanto o caso é apurado. Segundo a unidade, a médica é contratada pela empresa que presta serviços para a Organização Social (OS) responsável pela gestão da maternidade.

Quando o caso veio à tona, o hospital afirmou que as mensagens foram enviadas em um grupo interno e privado de médicos e constituem manifestações pessoais dos participantes, sem representar o posicionamento da administração da unidade.

A Secretaria Municipal de Saúde (SMS) de Goiânia informou que adotou medidas administrativas para apurar a conduta e reforçou às equipes a orientação de garantir atendimento adequado, ético e respeitoso a todos os pacientes do Sistema Único de Saúde (SUS).

O Conselho Regional de Medicina do Estado de Goiás (Cremego) informou que denúncias relacionadas à conduta ética de médicos são apuradas e tramitam em sigilo. O conselho também afirmou que solicita esclarecimentos ao médico responsável técnico pela instituição citada nas denúncias.

Leia a íntegra da nota divulgada pela médica:

"Peço desculpas às pacientes e às suas famílias, aos colegas, aos internos e ao hospital. Lamento profundamente que minhas mensagens tenham destoado do compromisso que sempre orientou minha atuação profissional.

Essas mensagens, porém, não se transformaram em conduta nem resultaram em procedimentos inadequados. Nenhuma paciente teve a alta atrasada ou negada. Todas foram avaliadas e liberadas exclusivamente por critérios clínicos, como sempre ocorreu.

Da mesma forma, nenhuma avaliação levou em conta preferência política. O voto é secreto e deve ser respeitado, sem qualquer tipo de retaliação.

Desde 2017, realizei milhares de partos de mulheres de diferentes origens e convicções. É esse compromisso que verdadeiramente orienta minha vida profissional.

articles.title: Feminicídio no RS: IGP cria núcleo para perícia especializada | G1
articles.standfirst: Equipes serão montadas em Porto Alegre e no interior para padronizar perícias, mapear casos e criar um banco de dados técnico.
articles.summary: O Nupefem vai padronizar a coleta de provas de feminicídio no RS e criar um banco de dados técnico para qualificar o combate à violência de gênero.
articles.body:
Após o Rio Grande do Sul chegar a 60 feminicídios neste ano , o Instituto-Geral de Perícias (IGP) c riou um núcleo especializado para mudar a forma como são produzidas provas nesses casos. O Núcleo de Perícias em Feminicídio (Nupefem), iniciativa pioneira no Brasil, pretende qualificar as investigações e produzir informações que auxiliem no combate à violência contra a mulher .

De acordo com o órgão, equipes estão sendo montadas em Porto Alegre e no interior do estado. Entre os objetivos do núcleo está a criação de protocolos específicos para o atendimento pericial de locais relacionados a feminicídios . O núcleo também deve padronizar os procedimentos de busca, documentação, interpretação, coleta e acondicionamento de vestígios .

A proposta é ampliar a análise das cenas dos crimes. Além dos vestígios que possam vincular uma pessoa ao local, os peritos buscarão elementos capazes de ajudar na reconstrução da dinâmica da violência.

A análise poderá identificar indícios relacionados ao histórico de violência contra a vítima, incluindo violência psicológica e simbólica, avaliação de riscos e outras formas de agressão que possam fazer parte do contexto do feminicídio .

Segundo a coordenadora do Nupefem, Juliane Lorencena Chassot, esses crimes apresentam vestígios e características que exigem uma atuação pericial específica.

"É um crime muito complexo, é um crime muito específico. Ele tem vestígios que a gente não encontra em outros locais, vestígios que são especificamente baseados no gênero, vestígios psicológicos, de violência simbólica, maus-tratos aos animais também tem, então tem que dar um outro olhar para esse tipo de crime, buscando sempre majorar essa pena e dar uma resposta para esse tipo de situação que é tão brutal", afirmou.

De acordo com Juliane e com a coordenadora-adjunta do núcleo, Luciana Farias Pereira, a especialização permitirá integrar diferentes áreas do conhecimento forense, aprimorar procedimentos e estabelecer protocolos adaptados às diferentes regiões do estado .

O núcleo prevê a articulação entre o Departamento de Criminalística, o Departamento Médico-Legal, o Departamento de Perícias Laboratoriais, o Departamento de Identificação e o Departamento de Perícias do Interior.

Outra atribuição do Nupefem será registrar, organizar, classificar e contabilizar informações periciais relacionadas aos feminicídios. O núcleo também ficará responsável por mapear os casos no Rio Grande do Sul e estabelecer um banco de dados técnico-pericial específico.

O núcleo poderá ainda promover capacitações para profissionais da perícia oficial e integrantes de outras instituições que participam da persecução penal. Também estão previstos intercâmbios técnico científicos com órgãos públicos, universidades e instituições de pesquisa.
