articles.title: FDA says it will complete safety review of abortion pill in March
articles.summary: A federal judge in Louisiana ordered the agency to provide an update on its safety study as part of a lawsuit seeking to overturn a provision allowing mifepristone to be delivered by mail.
articles.body: The Food and Drug Administration expects to complete its safety review of the abortion pill mifepristone in March, according to a court document the Justice Department filed Wednesday. In the filing, the FDA said it plans to compare mifepristone’s safety to that of surgical abortions through 10 weeks’ gestation. Its review will measure the frequency of side effects among roughly 100,000 women who took mifepristone, it said. Results of the FDA’s review are expected in mid-December. From there, the agency will analyze the data and draft a final report — a process it expects to wrap up in March. The FDA approved mifepristone in 2000, and hundreds of peer-reviewed studies have found it to be safe and effective. The FDA temporarily eliminated a requirement to dispense mifepristone in person in 2021, then finalized the change in 2023. It said Wednesday that it plans to re-evaluate that decision based on the new data it collects. It may weigh the views of patients, providers and pharmacists, as well as additional studies it did not consider in 2023. The review’s expected completion date falls months after the Nov. 3 midterm elections — when abortion access is among the concerns for voters. The update Wednesday is in response to an order by a federal judge in Louisiana for a progress report on the safety review. The FDA is a defendant in a Louisiana suit challenging its telehealth provision, which has largely been responsible for preserving nationwide access to abortion since the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022. Louisiana filed the case on behalf of a woman who said her boyfriend had ordered abortion pills and forced her to take them. In May, a federal appeals court granted Louisiana’s request to reinstate a nationwide requirement that mifepristone be dispensed in person. But the Supreme Court quickly blocked the decision while the case plays out. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. commissioned the safety review last year after a conservative think tank claimed to have found a higher rate of serious complications from mifepristone than the FDA reported. Several top Republicans, including Sen. Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, have also pressured the Trump administration to tighten access to the drug. Researchers who study reproductive health said the think tank’s findings, which were neither peer-reviewed nor published in a medical journal, amounted to junk science. A wealth of data has shown that less than 0.5% of women who take mifepristone have serious adverse reactions. It’s unclear what conclusion the FDA, which lacks a permanent commissioner, will draw from its new study. President Donald Trump’s pick to lead the FDA, Dr. Heidi Overton, a White House adviser, is a fierce opponent of abortion rights, having previously described medication abortion as “dangerous to women.” At her Senate confirmation hearing last month, Overton repeatedly sidestepped questions about mifepristone, including whether she believes the abortion pill is safe.

articles.title: Mum blamed for baby's death at Telford hospital calls for change in NHS
articles.summary: Neil and Katie Russell are working with the hospital where their daughter died on the scheme.
articles.body:
When Poppy Russell died shortly after birth, her parents were left bereft.

What followed made matters harder to bear - her mother was blamed for the death.

An inquest would later conclude that Poppy's death was preventable.

But instead of walking away from the trust that had failed them, Neil and Katie Russell are now working with it to bring compassionate care back into the NHS.

"We could have very easily been consumed by hate and anger and rage at what happened – and those feelings are still there," said Katie.

"But if no change comes from what happened to Poppy, then what's the point?"

Poppy Russell died in April 2021 at the Princess Royal Hospital in Telford.

During her pregnancy her mother told midwives that she had tokophobia, a fear of natural birth and wanted a caesarean section.

Katie said she was repeatedly told however that she "couldn't just ask for a c-section."

When she went into labour, Katie was induced and then "we were left in a room for long periods of time where I had no care," she explained.

"Finally, when we got into the labour suite, I wasn't monitored appropriately and they missed signs that Poppy was in distress."

In a bitter irony, Poppy had to be delivered by emergency caesarean.

By then however, she had developed a hypoxic brain injury and died later the same day.

The Shrewsbury and Telford NHS Trust (SaTH), which ran the hospital, subsequently blamed Katie for her daughter's death.

They said she had refused foetal monitoring; the inquest concluded that was untrue.

"The trust left us in an appalling position," said Neil Russell.

"Not only were they found to have neglected our care, but in the months and years following, we uncovered that members of staff had tried to cover it up.

Losing your daughter is one thing, but then to find that there was a cavalcade of lies was almost as bad."

Following the inquest in 2023 the trust said: "We recognise there were failings in the care we provided and we are truly sorry."

It said the death of any baby was a "tragedy" and promised improvements to maternity services.

In March 2024, the couple had a meeting with the trust to discuss all that had happened.

From the discussions, Neil and Katie decided they needed to honour Poppy.

"The first conversations about Poppy's Promise were about being human," said Neil, 45.

"It spun from our treatment, and not being treated like human beings."

Poppy's Promise is based on four care principles:

Acknowledgement - recognising a patient's feelings

Empowerment - involving patients in their care

"It's seeing the person, not the diagnosis. It's someone coming into a room holding your hand, someone acknowledging the fact that this is difficult for you," said Katie.

Even in the midst of her poor care at the time of her daughter's death, Katie, 41, vividly remembers one midwife who showed some compassion.

"She came in and said, 'how are you doing? I just want to hug you.'

"She sat with me and she cried with me and she said, 'this should never have happened,' and that will always stay with me because it's exactly what I needed at that point."

At the time of Poppy's death, SaTH was in the middle of a large maternity inquiry.

As part of its improvement programme, the trust is now rolling out Poppy's Promise to all 8,000 staff.

As well as reminding its existing employees of the principles of compassionate care, the trust has embedded a question about it into its recruitment processes.

The most important part of the training is "to remind me that we are here on a woman's journey, they are not on our journey," says Tasha Simmons, a midwifery ward manager at the trust.

"They don't need to know that I've answered three emergency bells this morning, that's not important to them.

"What's important is I'm fully present with them to support them in their experience, with kindness and compassion."

No-one starts a shift intending to provide care that is lacking in compassion.

The problem, say staff, is the pressure they are under - from the sheer number of people in Accident and Emergency to the complexity of many of the patients in hospital.

Remembering to treat each person with kindness in those circumstances can be a challenge, said Dr Adrian Walsh, an emergency medicine consultant at the Princess Royal Hospital.

There is a "high risk of emotional and compassion fatigue. Day in, day out we have a significant amount of competing demands," he said.

"But there's been some research done that actually demonstrates if people are treated with compassion and empathy, they have less complications, [their] outcomes are better."

Poppy's parents say that other NHS organisations and some universities have been in touch to explore whether they can incorporate Poppy's Promise into their teaching programme.

Their goal is to embed compassionate care throughout the health service.

articles.title: Thackray Museum of Medicine gains funding ahead of 30th anniversary
articles.summary: Leeds' Thackray Museum of Medicine says the grant will help it plan for the next three decades.
articles.body:
A medical museum in Leeds has secured £420,000 in funding ahead of its 30th anniversary next year.

Thackray Museum of Medicine has been awarded the money from grant organisations led by the National Lottery Heritage Fund.

The money will be spent on protecting the Grade II listed building and a new exhibition, which is due to open in February.

Edward Appleyard, from the museum, said he hoped the funding would enable them to have the "time and space to make Thackray even braver, more accessible and more sustainable for the future".

The museum opened in 1997 and is housed in a former Leeds Union Workhouse building next to St James's University Hospital.

It is is named after Charles Thackray, who developed his family-run chemist in Great George Street into a medical supply firm.

Since it reopened after a refit in 2021 , the museum has been a finalist for Art Fund Museum of the Year and was awarded a special commendation at the 2023 European Museum of the Year Awards for its work with the local community.

The funding would allow it to consider upgrading and replacing the roof of the building and potentially adding another floor to support "future programmes and partnerships", the museum said.

"We have such a good partnership with the NHS and the University of Leeds and I also want to make this a place that's for the people of Harehills," Appleyard said.

He said that when communities are suffering economic hardship they "need places like museums more than ever before".

"Yes, we hold amazing collections, but it's the stories we can tell through the people who we speak to that are so important - and that has changed so much since we opened these doors in 1997," he concluded.

articles.title: What to know about Kenya’s first Ebola case and how officials are responding
articles.summary: Kenya’s first Ebola case, a patient who travelled for weeks by road and air through three countries without being detected, has raised questions about border control and how to trace the virus across countries.
articles.body: NAIROBI, Kenya — Kenya’s first Ebola case, a patient who travelled for weeks by road and air through three countries without being detected until he arrived in Nairobi, has raised questions about border control and how to trace the virus across countries. The patient, a Kenyan man, had been living in Congo for seven years and started feeling ill a month ago. He had traveled by road to Uganda, before boarding a flight to the Kenyan capital on Saturday. There, he tested positive for the Ebola virus in a hospital and died Monday. The Africa CDC Director-General, Jean Kaseya, told The Associated Press in an interview on Tuesday that all stakeholders need to ask themselves how one case could have driven and flown to so many places without anyone noticing. “We need to ensure that at point of entry, we have a strong surveillance system in place,” he said. Ebola is highly contagious and spreads in the human population through contact with bodily fluids such as vomit, blood or semen, and with contaminated surfaces and materials such as bedding and clothing. Officials are trying to trace anyone who came into contact with the patient The Kenyan man drove for hours by road within Congo and across the border into Uganda. He boarded a local flight while in Congo, and it is unclear if he used any other forms of public transport. Authorities have looked at the flight manifest of the other flight he took from Kampala, Uganda, to Nairobi, and passengers and crew onboard have been added to the contact list. They’re also looking to trace workers who cleaned the plane after it landed, as well as passengers who traveled on the same plane subsequently. Health Minister Aden Duale told journalists on Wednesday that contact tracing was ongoing and that the number of contacts had risen to 57, with 10 already quarantined. “Even the people who cleaned that aircraft after it landed on Saturday, they are part of the people we are tracing. The immigration and the customs officials who served that patient will also be part of the contact tracing,” he said. Africa CDC’s Kaseya acknowledged it is a challenge. He said that the Kenyan man had not come up in existing contact lists in Congo. “Before saying that the outbreak is under control, you need to ensure that you have a contact list where all cases are coming from,” he said. Questions raised about how the patient traveled through Uganda It’s also unclear how the patient was able to cross into Uganda, which has closed its border with Congo because of the Ebola outbreak. Alan Kasujja, executive director of the Ugandan government’s media center, dismissed the question, saying only that journalists should instead ask Kenya how the man was able to bypass surveillance at its airport. “Leave Uganda out of this conversation. We don’t have Ebola here,” he wrote on X. Two of the man’s journeys were by air, while the rest were by road, covering long distances and passing through various towns and cities. On arrival in Nairobi, the patient underwent port health screening but his symptoms were not detected. He then boarded a private vehicle to Nairobi Hospital, where he was isolated and later tested positive for Ebola. When asked how the patient was able to travel through three countries undetected, Kenya’s Director-General for Health, Patrick Amoth, said on Wednesday that a meeting was scheduled with officials from Congo and Uganda and the Africa CDC to investigate what transpired during the patient’s journey. Kenya has been boosting its border controls Kenya’s Health Ministry has heightened surveillance at border entry points and created an Ebola hotline for citizens to report symptoms related to Ebola. The country has also designated five health facilities with a total of 241 isolation beds to manage patients, and is working to increase this capacity. The ministry said the country has enough supplies, including personal protective equipment, and has mobilized resources since the outbreak started in May in Congo. The ministry added that it had designated a specific gate at the country’s main airport for passengers travelling from 10 countries located within the outbreak’s epicenter.

articles.title: Doctor reveals 4 hidden health risks of spending too much time indoors
articles.summary: A Nature & Health Alliance survey finds nearly half of Americans spend under two hours outdoors weekly, fueling burnout, brain fog and belly fat.
articles.body: Nearly half of Americans spend less than two hours outdoors in an entire week, according to a new national survey from the Nature & Health Alliance involving researchers at Texas A&M University. Dr. John La Puma, a California physician and expert in nature-based medicine, has focused on the potential health impacts of spending less time outdoors. In his book, "Indoor Epidemic," he discusses how humans spend about 93% of their lives inside, which comes with a "hidden health tax." He claims the remedy is a simple 7% outdoor prescription. NEARLY 3 IN 4 AMERICANS ARE BATTLING THE SAME EXHAUSTING HEALTH PROBLEM, CDC REVEALS "Many people don't realize that they're inhibited from feeling as good as they can, because they're exhausted even after a full night's sleep," La Puma told Fox News Digital. "They need coffee to feel normal. They crash at 2 in the afternoon. They're wired at night. They can't go to sleep, but their labs are normal." "And they come into the office saying, ‘Why do I feel so exhausted?’ It's the four Bs," he said. The ‘4 Bs’ caused by too much indoor time No. 1: Bad sleep Outdoor light can be many times brighter than typical indoor lighting, La Puma noted, making it a powerful signal for setting the body’s internal clock, or circadian rhythm. "If you don't set your body clock, your body doesn't know what time it is, and it just goes to sleep whenever you can get to sleep instead of on time," he told Fox News Digital. SCIENTISTS REVEAL SURPRISINGLY EASY EXERCISE THAT MAY BOOST YOUR MOOD IN JUST 10 MINUTES Getting bright outdoor light soon after waking can help synchronize the body's sleep-wake cycle and support the natural rise in melatonin later in the evening, according to La Puma. He recommends spending about 10 minutes outdoors within the first hour of waking, without sunglasses. No. 2: Burnout La Puma uses the term "ultraprocessed time" to describe hours lost to screens, scrolling and other digital distractions. "Ultraprocessed time is kind of like ultraprocessed food," he said. "It’s not nutritious. It’s synthetic. It’s artificial. It’s ubiquitous." That includes time spent endlessly scrolling, he said, which can seem to simply "evaporate." La Puma argues that a person’s environment can contribute to burnout, rather than viewing it solely as a matter of willpower. AMERICA'S NATIONAL PARKS COULD ADD YEARS TO YOUR LIFE — HERE'S HOW THEY BOOST HEALTH Spending excessive time indoors can lead to an overload of screen exposure, he said, as people often turn to the same devices for work, entertainment and relaxation. He noted that the body may not interpret screen time as true rest or escape. "And equally important, no horizon. We are horizon-deprived as a species because indoors, we can't see more than 20 feet in front of us," La Puma said. "Your eyes need distance like your lungs need air." To combat burnout, he recommends getting up and going to the window and looking outside for a minute every hour. "It relaxes your eyes, relaxes the muscles around your temples, reduces headache if you have it, improves energy and reduces fatigue," he said. "That's the beginning of being able to reverse burnout." DOCTORS SAY 8 FORGOTTEN HABITS COULD HELP FIGHT STRESS, OBESITY AND CHRONIC DISEASE Simply going outside during the workday can help to reverse burnout, LaPuma said. "Your eyes need distance like your lungs need air." No. 3: Brain fog People who spend the day indoors may notice that they feel mentally foggy by the afternoon, La Puma said, particularly in poorly ventilated spaces where carbon dioxide can build up. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES Indoor CO₂ levels can climb above 1,000 parts per million in poorly ventilated spaces, and some research has linked elevated levels with reduced cognitive performance. "So it's not that you're just making bad decisions in the afternoons — there's a biologic reason for it," La Puma said. "What you need to do is cross-ventilate, but that's tough to do in an office or conference room." The doctor said that getting outdoors gives the eyes a chance to focus at greater distances while providing a break from potentially stuffy indoor air. The EPA notes that concentrations of some pollutants can be two to five times higher indoors than outdoors. No. 4: Belly fat When someone’s body clock is out of sync, it can disrupt the body’s normal cortisol rhythm, La Puma said. Cortisol, often called the stress hormone, naturally rises and falls throughout the day. Research has linked altered cortisol activity with greater abdominal and visceral fat, although the relationship is complex. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER "Again, the way to improve your metabolism is to get daylight at the right time, in the right place, for the right duration — early in the morning especially," La Puma advised. "This will give you a bump in cortisol, which you want early in the morning to feel awake, and then it drops appropriately." The 17-minute dose Most people spend about an hour outdoors each day as they walk from the car to the office, for example — but that's what La Puma calls "incidental time," not "biologically active time." To combat the four Bs, he recommends spending "intentional time" outdoors, "in a blue or green space," for a minimum effective dose of 17 minutes a day. "Be intentional with your time — look at the sky in the morning … to reset your body clock and watch the clouds," the doctor advised. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ For those who live in a big city and can’t see the sky, La Puma recommends looking at a distant rooftop, or looking through an open window when going outside isn’t possible. The goal is to focus beyond the confines of an indoor space. articles.title: Viola Davis Reveals She Was Diagnosed With Shingles
articles.summary: Viola Davis is opening up about the time she had shingles, and a blistering rash spread accross her body. Now, the actor is spreading awareness about prevention.
articles.body: At first, Viola Davis thought she had the flu. When the raised, painful rash that began on her stomach reappeared on her back, she told her husband she suspected a spider bite. Or, because she’s an avid gym-goer, maybe her weight belt was irritating her skin. Eventually, the actor learned she had shingles. The excruciating nerve pain, and the rashes and the blisters that emerged on her back were typical signs of the viral illness. In hindsight, Davis wishes she’d taken the time to figure out what was going on with her body sooner. “I would go from project (to project). I would end on a Friday and be on a plane on a Saturday, and on Sunday I would just be running, wearing myself down,” Davis tells TODAY.com. To top it all off, she’d recently become a mother to daughter Genesis, born in July 2010. Davis was — and still — in her prime. She was exercising, eating well and felt fulfilled. Despite her lifestyle, however, Davis was the perfect candidate for shingles. The infection is caused by the varicella-zoster virus, also known for causing chickenpox, which Davis had as a child. Once you recover from chickenpox, the virus lies dormant in the body and can reactivate later in life, particularly in those over 50 years old, which Davis was. It’s also more common in those with weakened immune systems, according to the Cleveland Clinic. Once the virus is reactivated, it causes rashes, fever and chills, stomach upset, blisters, itching and tingling, and headaches, among other symptoms. There’s no cure, but patients can take antiviral medications to manage symptoms, over-the-counter painkillers and corticosteroids, according to the Cleveland Clinic. And to reduce your risk, you can get vaccinated, even if you’ve already had shingles, to reduce your likelihood of contracting it again. Davis knew “nothing, zero, zilch,” she says, about shingles until it happened to her, which made her want to speak out about it. “I felt like I was just going to be the mouthpiece for it because it was something that sort of made me wake up to the fact that I have to listen to my body,” she says. “That was for me one of those aha-moments in life.” Davis is partnering with GSK, a biopharma company, for its “Shingles, actually” campaign to encourage people over 50 to speak with doctors and pharmacists about their increased risk of shingles and how to prevent it. When Davis’ symptoms began, she recalls the spread of the “enormous” rash and ranked her pain a 9 out of 10. “I had never seen anything like that before. But you know, at the same time, I’d never been that age before,” she recalls, and getting older, she later discovered, would require a renewed perspective on health and wellness. Strength isn’t about ignoring the things that make you feel fragile, says Davis. “You are valuable and important enough to see that if something feels like it’s not right, then it’s not right, and do not see it as sort of a sign of weakness,” she adds.

articles.title: 6 High-Fiber Fall Foods for Better Gut Health, Recommended by a GI Doctor
articles.summary: In TODAY.com’s Expert Tip of the Day, a gastroenterologist reveals her top high-fiber fall fruits and vegetables to support gut health.
articles.body: Taking care of your gut health doesn’t have to be complicated or involve fancy supplements. It often boils down to a simple habits, including eating more fiber every day and diversifying your plant food sources, according to Dr. Trisha Pasricha, gastroenterologist and director of the Institute for Gut-Brain Research at Beth Israel Deaconness. Walking around the produce aisle or farmer’s market this fall, you may be overwhelmed with delicious options to help you meet your fiber intake goals. Which ones pack the biggest fiber punch? Pasricha joined TODAY on Thursday, Oct. 7, to share some of her favorite gut-healthy seasonal fruits and vegetables to add to your diet this fall. Gut Health Tip of the Day: Add These 6 High-Fiber Foods to Your Grocery Cart This Fall Fall is one of the best times of year to enjoy plant foods, thanks to the autumn harvest. “There’s so much seasonal produce for the fall, but here are my 6 fiber all-stars,” says Pasricha. Canned pumpkin: 7 grams of fiber per servingPears (with skin): 5-6 grams of fiber per servingBrussels sprouts: 6.4 grams of fiber per servingApples (with skin): 4.5 grams of fiber per servingSweet potato (with skin): 4 grams of fiber per servingPomegranate seeds: 4 grams of fiber per serving Why It Matters The majority of Americans don’t eat enough fiber. That’s because the typical U.S. diet is higher in processed foods and lower in whole plant-based foods naturally rich in this nutrient. Our bodies don’t actually digest fiber, but that’s part of why it’s so beneficial. Instead of getting broken down and absorbed in our digestive tract, the fiber goes to the large intestine, where it acts as food for the good bacteria lining it — aka, our microbiome. “We need fiber to feed our gut,” Pasricha says. These microbes ferment the fiber, producing short-chain fatty acids. These can feed the colon cells and improve digestive health, help control blood sugar and help lower the risk of heart disease and dementia, Pasricha explains. Eating a variety of whole fruits and vegetables ensures that you get both types of fiber (soluble and insoluble fiber), which each benefit the gut in different ways — plus, a host of other nutrients that support our health. How to Get Started First, figure out how much fiber you should be eating. Adult women should aim to get at least 25 grams of fiber per day, while adult men need at least 38 grams per day. If you do the fiber math, that breaks down to about 10–15 grams per meal and 3-5 grams at each snack, TODAY.com reported previously. All of Pasricha’s favorite gut-healthy fall foods offer at least 4 grams of fiber per serving. Here are some easy ways to incorporate these into your diet: Mix one cup of canned pumpkin into oatmeal, pancakes or soups.Snack on pears with nut butter.Add one-half cup of pomegranate seeds to smoothies or yogurt bowls.Slice up your favorite fall apple variety with the skin.Roast Brussels sprouts or shave them raw into salads.Bake a sweet potato in the skin for a hearty side dish. When increasing your fiber intake, it’s important to go slow and make sure you’re drinking enough water, Pasricha notes. TODAY’s Expert Tip of the Day series is all about simple strategies to make life a little easier. Every Monday through Friday, different qualified experts share their best advice on diet, fitness, heart health, mental wellness and more.
